newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Rotterdam port says still open despite deep freeze.
newsitem.headline: Rotterdam port says still open despite deep freeze.

text.p: The port of Rotterdam remained open for shipping despite the continuing deep freeze, a port authority spokesman said on Thursday.
"There's not a problem to moor or unmoor. When a barge or ship has problems with ice, they can ask our patrol vessels to break the ice," a port authority spokesman said.
Earlier on Thursday, barge operators and traders said jetties at many installations were out-of-bounds.
"Many barges have asked us to help them to moor or unmoor and mostly its no problem," the port authority spokesman added.
Oil refiners in the Rotterdam area said ice was becoming increasingly troublesome, but they were still able to deliver oil products and to load and unload vessels.

"There is indeed some ice in the harbour near our jetties. It's not as easy (to moor) as usual, but it's not insurmountable," said an Esso Nederland spokesman, referring to the company's Rotterdam refinery.
"There is nothing exceptional at either of our refineries," a Nerefco refinery spokeswoman said.
Traders and barge operators had earlier said that the Maas, the river along which the industrial core of Rotterdam is based, was becoming increasingly ice-bound.
"We cannot reach the jetties. This is all along the Maas, until Europoort. There at least it's salt water," a barge operator said.

"I've just spoken to a barge owner who said that he's taken two and a half hours for a distance that is normally 30 minutes due to the ice in Rotterdam. I also hear parts of Pernis and Botlek are closed because of ice. Many German operators say they just won't come to the Netherlands," said another operator.
Europoort, at the coast, handles crude oil discharges and is also the site of one of Nerefco's two Rotterdam-based refineries as well as the Kuwait Petroleum plant.
The other Nerefco refinery and those of Esso and Shell lie further upstream in fresh water more affected by ice.
Nerefco is a joint venture between Texaco and British Petroleum
Traders largely agreed that the cold and ice were increasingly afflicting Rotterdam which has so far escaped the problems of other Dutch and Belgian ports.
"The problems are increasing every day and it means further delays and disruption (for barges), but not that product cannot be loaded or blended," said one Rotterdam-based trader.
A number of industry sources said that suppliers were looking at or using alternative means of transportation.
The majors, unlike independents, are able to deliver product to Germany by Rhine-Main-Ruhr (RMR) pipeline.
"Although it's not possible, you could say we are using it 200 percent," said a trader at a Rotterdam-based major.
Other product has taken to the roads. A Shell spokesman said that much of its gasoline supplies were now transported by trucks.
Dutch oil analyst Pieter Kulsen commented that fewer and fewer barges were being fixed and that competition among land-based transporters was hotting up.
"However, it looks like there may be more (barge) business from the fifteenth (of January)," he said.

The Rhine itself remains largely clear of problems, although on Thursday Dutch water inspectors RIZA said there was 40 percent medium to heavy ice cover on one of its two larger branches downstream of Gorinchem.

Canal routes from Rotterdam to Antwerp was still kept open by ice breakers, while the Amsterdam-Rhine canal was navigable without extra support, although only for vessels with a drive of at least one horsepower per tonne.
